newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Traders see mixed fortunes from Nigerian mergers.
newsitem.headline: Traders see mixed fortunes from Nigerian mergers.

text.p: Managers of companies that merged in 1996 in Nigeria hope to consolidate their positions next year but traders said on Monday the mergers held mixed fortunes.
Four major quoted companies successfully swallowed others in 1996 and a fifth merger is all but completed.
Traders said investor-friendly policies of the military government were responsible for the spate of mergers which effectively brought their businesses under one management.

"After government removed the hurdles in the way of foreign investors, these companies saw no need to continue to operate their subsidiaries independently with the cost implications," said stock market dealer Chuks Ohanwusi.
But James Odife of Centre-Point Investments Ltd said the mergers held mixed blessings for Nigerian shareholders.
"Nigerian shareholders are not consulted before major decisions are taken. Most of the decisions are taken at their European headquarters and are just implemented here," he said.
However, stock exchange senior official Rasaki Oladejo said the market should see increased volumes of traded shares, earnings and bonus issues from the mergers.
Chief among the mergers of 1996 was Lever Brothers which acquired Unilever Nigeria Ltd.
Nestle Foods swallowed Nestle Nigeria Ltd, while Smithkline Beecham bought Sterling Products and Nigerian Bottling Company took over Sapanda Industries, a local bottler of its range of soft drinks.
The integration of PZ Industries with its associate Thermocool is expected to be sealed soon.
Before its merger with Lever Brothers, Unilever's A.J. Seward was 100 percent into personal products compared to 30 percent in Lever Brothers.
The acquisition was expected to significantly improve profitability and cash generating capacity at Lever Brothers, company executives said.
The Nigerian Bottling Company's purchase of Sapanda was aimed at helping the Coca-Cola bottler strengthen its presence in eastern Nigeria where the Sapanda plant is located.
By acquiring Sterling Products, Smithkline Beecham is clearly the biggest pharmaceutical company in Nigeria with turnover of about eight billion naira, traders said.
"It means we can offer more and do it better," chief executive Jay Drosin said last week. "We can also enjoy economies of scale."
Analysts said such benefits would take sometime to come in view of the harsh economic environment in Nigeria.
Latest results from some of these companies have shown falling profits.
For the nine-month period to end-September 1996, Smithkline Beecham's after-tax profit dipped to 172.9 million against 189.1 million naira in the correponding period of 1995.
Lever Brothers said its own nine-month net profit was one billion naira to end-september 1996, down from 1.1 billion naira in the nine months to end-September 1995.

Nigerian Bottling Company, on the other hand, said its half-year result to end-June showed a six percent increase in after-tax profits to 678.9 million naira compared to 637.8 million naira in the first half of 1995.
PZ too reported a profit rise for the first three months to end-August 1996. Profit after tax was 316.8 million naira against 267.8 in a similar 1995 period.
($1=80 naira)
